propositions.text: The appellant is XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Burundi, appealing the RPD decision dated January 9, 2019.
propositions.quote: The appellant, XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Burundi, is appealing against the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision dated January 9, 2019.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant, XXXX XXXX from Burundi, appeals the RPD decision dated January 9, 2019, as stated by the court.

propositions.text: The appeal is allowed; the RAD sets aside the RPD determination and finds the appellant is a Convention refugee.
propositions.quote: The appeal is allowed. The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes the determination that, in its opinion, should have made, namely, that the appellant is a Convention refugee.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal, sets aside the RPD decision, and finds the appellant is a Convention refugee.

propositions.text: The appellant is a Tutsi who joined the XXXX party in 2013 while studying in Uganda and recruited members.
propositions.quote: The appellant is a Tutsi who became a member of the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX party on XXXX XXXX, 2013, while he was studying in Uganda.

propositions.text: After returning to Burundi, Imbonerakure militants arrested two colleagues; appellant feared arrest and fled.
propositions.quote: After he returned to Burundi, Imbonerakure militants went to his XXXX neighbourhood on XXXX XXXX, 2016, and arrested two of his XXXX colleagues. Out of fear of being arrested himself, he took steps to leave the country.

propositions.text: Appellant was named under torture; a friend warned him police sought him; he hid and left with a Canadian visa in 2018.
propositions.quote: According to the family of one of the detained individuals, the appellant was named under torture. On January 5, 2018, a friend told him not to go home because Imbonerakure and police officers had gone there to get him. He hid until he left the country with a Canadian visa on XXXX XXXX, 2018.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant, a Tutsi and XXXX party member, fled Burundi fearing arrest after militants detained colleagues and police sought him, leaving with a Canadian visa.

propositions.text: The RPD rejected the claim due to credibility issues: vague testimony on political activities, no party card, no evidence efforts, vague policy and recruitment testimony.
propositions.quote: The RPD rejected the claim for the following reasons:1 i) The appellant's testimony was vague regarding his political activities in Uganda. ii) No reasonable explanation was given for the fact that the original XXXX party membership card was not provided. iii) The appellant made no reasonable effort to obtain evidence of his political activities in Uganda. iv) The appellant's testimony regarding the XXXX policies and platform was vague. v) The appellant's testimony on his recruitment and fundraising work was vague.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD rejected the claim due to vague testimony, missing party card, no evidence efforts, and vague policy and recruitment testimony.

propositions.text: The RPD breached natural justice by not expressing its concerns and disregarding the letter confirming party membership.
propositions.quote: Did the RPD breach natural justice by failing to express the concerns on which it based itself? The RPD disregarded the letter from the XXXX president confirming the appellant's membership in the party.

propositions.text: The RPD's credibility assessment is unreasonable and ignores evidence of appellant's party membership.
propositions.quote: Is the RPD's credibility assessment unreasonable, based on incorrect plausibility findings, or unreasonable, given that the RPD did not take into account the evidence that the appellant was a member of the XXXX?

propositions.text: The RPD erred by failing to assess objective risk; appellant as Tutsi and party member faces objective risk.
propositions.quote: Did the RPD err in failing to assess the objective risk or, if the RAD should substitute a decision, does the appellant have an objective risk? As a Tutsi and XXXX member, the appellant is subjected to an objective risk. The RPD did not analyze this risk.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant alleges the RPD breached natural justice, made an unreasonable credibility assessment, and failed to assess objective risk.

propositions.text: The correctness standard of review is applied because the RPD had no meaningful advantage over the RAD.
propositions.quote: I applied the correctness standard of review. In this case, the RPD did not enjoy a meaningful advantage over the RAD.2

paragraphs.summary: The court applies the correctness standard of review as the RPD had no meaningful advantage over the RAD.

propositions.text: The appellant requests admission of evidence under IRPA subsection 110(4) and a hearing under subsection 110(6).
propositions.quote: The appellant is requesting the admission of a piece of evidence that is described in subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and a document that was provided after the appeal record was perfected. He is also asking that a hearing be held pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant requests admission of evidence under IRPA 110(4) and a hearing under 110(6).

propositions.text: A digital audio recording and transcript of the hearing are available on the appeal record.
propositions.quote: A digital audio recording of the hearing is available, as is a transcript that is on the appeal record.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes a digital audio recording and transcript of the hearing are available on the appeal record.

propositions.text: The National Documentation Package before the RPD is dated April 30, 2018; affidavit submitted after appeal record is not admissible.
propositions.quote: The version of the National Documentation Package (NDP) before the RPD is dated April 30, 2018. The affidavit submitted after the filing of the appeal record is not admissible

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the NDP before the RPD is dated April 30, 2018; affidavit submitted after appeal record is inadmissible.

propositions.text: Appellant submitted an affidavit from XXXX XXXX, party president, confirming appellant's active membership and recruitment in Uganda and Canada.
propositions.quote: The appellant submitted an affidavit from XXXX XXXX, president of the XXXX, after the appeal record was filed. Mr. XXXX confirms that he authored the letter filed with the RPD. He was able to verify with local members that the appellant was an active party member. The appellant recruited new members among the Burundians in Uganda while he was studying there. He continues to be a member in Canada.3

paragraphs.summary: The appellant submitted an affidavit from the party president confirming active membership and recruitment in Uganda and Canada.

propositions.text: The appellant failed to meet rule 29 requirements for late affidavit admission, including explaining why it was not submitted earlier.
propositions.quote: However, he did not address the requirements set out under rule 29. Specifically, he failed to explain why the affidavit could not be obtained and submitted with the record.

propositions.text: The affidavit was received nine months late without adequate explanation, violating rule 29 requirements.
propositions.quote: The RAD received the affidavit on November 28, 2019, without any explanation for the delay other than that the document was under the control of a third party.

propositions.text: Under subrule 29(4), RAD must consider relevance, probative value, contribution, and whether document could have been provided earlier.
propositions.quote: Under subrule 29(4), the RAD must consider any relevant factors, including its relevance and probative value, what the document brings to the appeal, and whether, with reasonable effort, the document could have been provided with the appeal record.

propositions.text: All factors were addressed except the effort to obtain the affidavit before filing the record.
propositions.quote: All the factors were addressed, except for the issue of efforts made to obtain it before the record was filed.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant failed to explain late affidavit submission under rule 29; all factors considered except effort to obtain affidavit earlier.

propositions.text: A few months' delay is understandable due to author living in Belgium, but nine months without explanation is not.
propositions.quote: Given that the author lives in Belgium, a late filing of a few months is understandable. However, a delay of nine months without an explanation is not.

propositions.text: The affidavit is inadmissible due to non-compliance with rule 29.
propositions.quote: The document is not admissible on grounds of non-compliance with rule 29.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the nine-month unexplained delay inadmissible under rule 29 and excludes the affidavit.

propositions.text: Appellant filed a letter from the XXXX representative in Canada confirming the original membership card is genuine and appellant is a party member in Toronto.
propositions.quote: The appellant filed a letter from the XXXX representative in Canada on the appeal record.4 The author examined the original membership card and confirmed that it is genuine. The appellant is a party member in Toronto and began attending events shortly after his arrival.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant filed a letter from the Canadian party representative confirming genuine membership card and appellant's party membership in Toronto.

propositions.text: IRPA subsection 110(4) limits evidence to that arising after claim rejection or not reasonably available then.
propositions.quote: Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA states that "the person who is the subject of the appeal may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection."5

propositions.text: In Singh, FCA held credibility, relevance and newness must be considered; new evidence can contradict RPD fact or credibility findings.
propositions.quote: In addition, in Singh, the Federal Court of Appeal held that credibility, relevance and newness must be taken into account.6 Evidence may be new if it is capable of contradicting a finding of fact made by the RPD, including a credibility finding.7

paragraphs.summary: The court states IRPA 110(4) limits evidence to new or unavailable evidence; Singh requires considering credibility, relevance, and newness.

propositions.text: Appellant argues the letter and membership card are new evidence contradicting unexpected negative credibility findings.
propositions.quote: In this case, the appellant filed a letter of support from the XXXX president with a copy of his identity card. The original copy of the letter was submitted at the hearing. A photocopy of his membership card was also submitted. The appellant could not reasonably have expected that the original letter from the president would be disregarded and that his membership card would not be accepted as genuine. This document is admissible as new evidence because it contradicts an unanticipated negative credibility finding.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the letter and membership card are new evidence contradicting unexpected negative credibility findings.

propositions.text: The new evidence is credible, relevant, probative, and does not raise credibility issues; no hearing required under IRPA 110(6).
propositions.quote: This new evidence is from a credible source, is relevant and has significant probative value because it contradicts a negative finding of fact by the RPD. Given that the document does not raise an issue with respect to the appellant's credibility, a hearing is not required pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the new evidence credible, relevant, probative, and no hearing is required under IRPA 110(6).

propositions.text: The RPD found no documentary evidence corroborating political work in Uganda; appellant's explanation was vague and evasive.
propositions.quote: In the RPD's view, the appellant did not present any documentary evidence to corroborate his political work in Uganda. His explanation for the lack of documentary evidence was vague and evasive.

propositions.text: Appellant left documents in Uganda fearing danger but made no effort to obtain them in Canada, undermining credibility.
propositions.quote: He testified that he left all the documents in Uganda because they would have put him in danger in Burundi. However, this does not explain why he made no effort to obtain them after he arrived in Canada. This factor undermines his credibility.

propositions.text: University attestations from Uganda are not genuine due to different stickers; visa was rejected over school record genuineness concerns.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the university attestations from Uganda are not genuine because the stickers are different on each document. A Canadian visa application was rejected because of concerns as to the genuineness of the school records.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found no corroborating evidence for political work, appellant's explanation vague, documents not genuine, and visa rejected over school record concerns.

propositions.text: Appellant says the transcript error was typographical and did not prevent visa issuance or university admission; RPD did not question transcript genuineness at hearing.
propositions.quote: According to the appellant, this was a typographical error (transcripts) that did not prevent a visa from being issued in 2018 or his admission to a Canadian university. In addition, the RPD did not question the genuineness of the transcript at the hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the transcript error was typographical and did not prevent visa or university admission; RPD did not question genuineness at hearing.

propositions.text: The court agrees the transcript concern should have been addressed and different seals on documents have many possible explanations.
propositions.quote: I agree that this concern should have been addressed at the hearing. Furthermore, this error has nothing to do with the seals. As the appellant notes, there are many reasons why different seals may have been used on different documents.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees the transcript concern should have been addressed and different seals have many possible explanations.

propositions.text: The appellant reasonably explained not bringing documents to Burundi and relying on party president's letter and membership card in Canada.
propositions.quote: The appellant provided a reasonable explanation for not having brought back XXXX documents to Burundi. He took no steps to obtain them after he arrived in Canada because he was relying on the letter of attestation from the party president and his membership card.

propositions.text: Failure to obtain supporting documents is not serious enough to justify negative credibility inference given all circumstances.
propositions.quote: Although the appellant would have been wise to try to obtain all the relevant supporting documents, the fact that he failed to do so is not sufficiently serious, in light of all the circumstances, to justify a negative inference being drawn with respect to his credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellant's explanation reasonable and failure to obtain documents not serious enough to justify negative credibility inference.

propositions.text: The appellant left his original membership card at home in Toronto.
propositions.quote: The appellant had left his original XXXX membership card at home in Toronto.

propositions.text: The RPD found this does not reasonably explain the absence of the original card given other originals were brought and legal representation.
propositions.quote: In the opinion of the RPD, this does not reasonably explain the absence of the original, given that he had brought the originals of the other documents and was represented by a specialized lawyer.

propositions.text: The appellant did not request authorization to submit the original after the hearing, undermining his credibility.
propositions.quote: The appellant did not ask for authorization to submit the original after the hearing. This significantly undermines his credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the appellant's explanation for missing original card unreasonable and his credibility undermined for not requesting post-hearing submission.

propositions.text: The RPD breached natural justice by not informing him the card's genuineness was questioned.
propositions.quote: The appellant argues that the RPD breached the principles of natural justice by failing to inform him that this was an issue that called into question the genuineness of the card.

propositions.text: He should not have to guess the panel's concerns to request admission after the hearing.
propositions.quote: The appellant should not be expected to have read the panel's mind in order to ask that it be admitted after the hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RPD breached natural justice by not informing him about the card issue and expecting him to guess the panel's concerns.

propositions.text: The RPD should have raised the card issue so the appellant knew it would be rejected otherwise.
propositions.quote: The RPD should have raised the issue in order for the appellant to know that his card would otherwise be rejected.

propositions.text: The RPD disregarded the original letter from the XXXX president with the appellant's identity card.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the RPD disregarded the original copy of the letter from the XXXX president with his identity card.

propositions.text: The RPD failed to consider the letter from the mother of the detained and killed colleague.
propositions.quote: The RPD also failed to take into account the letter from the mother of the colleague who was detained on XXXX XXXX, 2016, and killed on XXXX XXXX, 2017.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD should have raised the card issue and improperly disregarded important letters as evidence.

propositions.text: The appellant claimed political activity from 2013 to 2017.
propositions.quote: The appellant claimed that he was politically active between 2013 and his departure from Burundi in 2017.

propositions.text: The RPD found his testimony about the XXXX platform vague and insufficiently explained fundraising and recruitment.
propositions.quote: In the view of the RPD, his testimony regarding the XXXX platform was vague. He was unable to explain the party's specific policies. He did not provide a reasonable explanation for how he raised funds. He was vague with respect to the number of people recruited for the party.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the appellant's political activity testimony vague and lacking explanation on policies, fundraising, and recruitment.

propositions.text: The RPD's conclusion that his testimony was vague and insufficient is unclear and erred given lack of evidence.
propositions.quote: The appellant argues that it is unclear as to how the RPD concluded that his testimony was vague and insufficient. It also erred in assessing plausibility considering the lack of evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RPD erred in finding his testimony vague and insufficient and in assessing plausibility without evidence.

propositions.text: The RPD asked open-ended questions and received adequate, reasonable responses from the appellant.
propositions.quote: The RPD asked several open-ended questions and received an adequate response to each of them. His responses were reasonable.

propositions.text: It is unfair to call testimony vague after only one question per subject and detailed responses.
propositions.quote: It is unfair to conclude that his testimony was vague after asking a single question on each subject, given the detailed responses that were given.

propositions.text: If more details were needed, the RPD should have asked further questions.
propositions.quote: If the RPD wanted more details, it should have asked.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD's vague testimony conclusion unfair given reasonable answers and insufficient questioning.

propositions.text: The appellant's testimony was spontaneous, detailed, consistent, and supported by letters and attestation.
propositions.quote: The appellant's responses were spontaneous and reasonably detailed. His testimony was consistent and supported by letters from the XXXX president and his colleague's mother. Furthermore, the attestation of the XXXX representative in Canada confirms his membership in the party.

propositions.text: The RPD did not justify rejecting the appellant's testimony or supporting evidence and disregarded important evidence without explanation.
propositions.quote: The RPD did not justify its rejection of his testimony or the genuineness of the supporting evidence. The RPD also disregarded important evidence without explanation.

propositions.text: The court independently finds the appellant credible and the evidence likely genuine.
propositions.quote: My independent assessment leads me to find that the appellant is credible and that the evidence on the record is likely genuine.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant credible, supported by evidence, and that the RPD unjustifiably rejected testimony and disregarded evidence.

propositions.text: The appellant presented a summary of Burundi's political situation and evidence of treatment of XXXX members.
propositions.quote: The appellant presented a summary of the political situation in Burundi. Specifically, a Response to Information Request concerning the treatment of XXXX members establishes an objective basis for his subjective fear.

propositions.text: Human Rights Watch reports opposition members arrested, ill-treated, detained without warrants in Burundi.
propositions.quote: Human Rights Watch states that "'[s]cores of opposition party members have been arrested, ill-treated, and illegally detained, and other detainees taken to unknown destinations,' yet arrest warrants were almost never produced by the police."

propositions.text: The appellant's Tutsi ethnicity aggravates his risk of persecution.
propositions.quote: The fact that he is an ethnic Tutsi is an aggravating factor.

propositions.text: There is a serious possibility the appellant would be arrested and seriously ill-treated to persecution level.
propositions.quote: There is a serious possibility that the appellant would be arrested and seriously ill-treated to the point of persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant presented evidence of Burundi's political repression and his Tutsi ethnicity increases his serious risk of persecution.

propositions.text: Government agents are persecutors, so state protection is unavailable and risk is countrywide.
propositions.quote: Given that the agents of persecution represent the government, state protection is not available and the risk is present throughout the country.

propositions.text: There is a nexus between the appellant's situation and the Convention refugee definition on political opinion grounds.
propositions.quote: There is a nexus between his situation and the definition of a Convention refugee on the ground of political opinion.

propositions.text: The appellant has a well-founded fear of persecution.
propositions.quote: The appellant has a well-founded fear of persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no state protection, a nexus to political opinion, and a well-founded fear of persecution for the appellant.

propositions.text: The appellant tried to raise persecution risk based on Tutsi ethnicity separately from political activities.
propositions.quote: The appellant tried to raise the issue of persecution based on his Tutsi ethnicity separately from his political activities.

propositions.text: The appellant did not mention this risk in his Basis of Claim Form or at the hearing.
propositions.quote: The appellant does not mention this risk in his Basis of Claim Form and it was not raised at the hearing.

propositions.text: The RPD did not err on this issue.
propositions.quote: The RPD did not err on this issue.

propositions.text: The issue was not new for appeal purposes and the submission is rejected.
propositions.quote: Given that this issue could reasonably be expected to have been raised at the hearing, it is not new for the purposes of the appeal. This submission is rejected.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant's separate ethnicity claim was not raised earlier; the RPD did not err and the court rejects the submission as not new.

propositions.text: The appeal is allowed and the RAD sets aside the RPD's determination, finding the appellant a Convention refugee.
propositions.quote: The appeal is allowed. Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(b) of the IRPA, the RAD sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes the determination that, in its opinion, should have been made, namely, that the appellant is a Convention refugee.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal, sets aside the RPD decision, and finds the appellant a Convention refugee.
